rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the full elution window while limiting late-elution penalties. This scouting run will identify critical pairs and guide gradient-window and temperature refinement.
Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the two critical pairs respond to reduced slope. The current last-peak time leaves room to improve resolution without exceeding 10 minutes.

Raise the starting organic fraction to remove low-organic time while making the gradient shallower at the same duration. This should further separate the slope-responsive critical pair and bring the last peak earlier, with sufficient retention remaining for the first peak.

Reduce the slope one more step to push the remaining critical pair toward R ≥ 1.5. The last peak at 8.62 minutes leaves enough headroom for this modest extension to potentially achieve full resolution before 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a 5 °C temperature increase to shorten elution while preserving full resolution. Keeping the gradient unchanged isolates the temperature response of the critical pair.

Test whether higher temperature carries the critical pair through its apparent selectivity crossover and restores separation in reversed order. A shorter gradient also targets faster elution, while injection 4 remains the maximum-score fallback.

At 55 °C the earlier critical cluster is resolved, leaving a different pair at R = 1.10. A shallower gradient will test whether that pair can reach full resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Use an intermediate slope between injections 6 and 7 to shorten elution while targeting R ≥ 1.5 for both critical pairs. The lower endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to trim early low-organic time and reduce gradient slope. This tests whether faster elution can preserve both critical separations without compressing the first pair excessively.

Lowering the starting organic fraction may improve the pair that deteriorated at phi0 = 0.20 and restore ample early-peak retention. Combine this with a shorter gradient to seek full resolution at a faster last-peak time, retaining injection 8 as the faster maximum-score fallback.

Lengthen injection 10’s gradient one step to bring the remaining R = 1.29 pair above 1.5. This should retain a substantial time advantage over injection 8 while checking that the other close pair remains resolved.

Narrow the gradient window to obtain a slope between injections 10 and 11, targeting full resolution with earlier final elution. The endpoint remains well above the last peak’s estimated elution fraction, so all peaks should remain inside the gradient.

Increase the slope slightly from injection 12 to shorten elution while targeting R just above 1.5 for the limiting pair. The endpoint of 0.75 remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Explore a faster high-temperature regime to see whether the remaining close pair separates after another selectivity crossover. Injection 13 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback while this run tests substantially shorter elution.

Shorten the gradient to test whether the apparent reversed-order critical pair at 60 °C gains separation with increasing slope. This also targets faster elution, while the neighboring pairs currently have some resolution margin.

Explore the opposite temperature limit to seek a different selectivity pattern that permits a faster fully resolved gradient. The strong temperature response already observed makes this a useful alternative to further compressing the marginal 60 °C separation.

Return to the productive 55 °C regime and lower only the starting fraction relative to injection 10. This tests whether improved selectivity in the earlier critical pair can support a steeper, faster gradient without losing resolution in the later pair.

Test an intermediate temperature with a fast gradient to seek a better balance between the two temperature-sensitive critical pairs. Injection 17 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback; this run explores whether full resolution is possible substantially earlier.
Increase the slope slightly from injection 17 to test the speed limit of the fastest fully resolved regime. This brackets whether its two marginal pairs can retain R ≥ 1.5 with earlier final elution.

Test a moderate lower temperature for a faster alternative to the fully resolved 40 °C method. Cooling should move the temperature-sensitive critical pair away from its 45 °C crossover, while this run checks whether neighboring pairs retain adequate separation.

Trim injection 17’s unused high-organic tail while preserving its starting fraction and gradient slope. The last peak should still elute before the gradient ends, retaining full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a slightly shallower gradient near the successful injection 11 to assess the resolution margin of its weakly slope-responsive pair. This seeks another maximum-score method with all peaks comfortably before 10 minutes, while retaining injection 21 as the fastest confirmed option.

Test whether trimming the low-organic start of injection 4 shortens elution while preserving its full resolution. At 40 °C the early peaks should retain more strongly than in the unsuccessful 55 °C high-start trial, though both early and central separations need checking.

Slightly reduce injection 23’s slope to lift its sole unresolved pair from R = 1.35 toward full resolution. The last peak at 9.02 minutes leaves some room for the added retention while maintaining the maximum CRF.

Use a slope between the fully resolved injections 7 and 8 to target balanced resolution margins while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. The maximum CRF is already secured; injections 17 and 21 remain the fastest confirmed fully resolved methods.
